title: At Nuremberg, a conviction needed three of the four judges, so a 2–2 split meant acquittal
body: On 1 October 2026 it was 80 years since the [judgment of the International Military Tribunal](https://case.edu/law/about/events-lectures/legacy-nuremberg-international-conference-commemorating-80th-anniversary-nuremberg-judgment) at Nuremberg, the court that France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States set up in 1945 to try the surviving leaders of Nazi Germany. Each of the four powers named a judge and a deputy, and only the judges voted. Under the tribunal’s [charter](https://avalon.law.yale.edu/imt/imtconst.asp), most decisions needed a simple majority, with the President’s vote breaking a tie, but a conviction or a sentence needed at least three of the four votes. The 22 defendants faced up to four counts: conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity, and the Holocaust was a major focus of the evidence. Nineteen were found guilty on at least one count: twelve were sentenced to death, three to life in prison and four to 10 to 20 years. Three were acquitted, according to historians because the judges split, and the Soviet judge, Iona Nikitchenko, dissented, saying all three should have been convicted.

slides.question: The Nuremberg tribunal tried 22 Nazi leaders in 1945–46. How many did it find guilty on at least one count?
slides.explanation: 19 of the 22. Three were acquitted: on each of them, fewer than three of the four judges voted guilty.

slides.alt: Animation on dark courtroom wood: 80 years, then the bench of four seats for the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union and France, the dock of 22 seats, the four counts, ballots showing three of four votes to convict, a verdict grid with the three acquitted named, and the sentences.

slides.prompt: Tap the four judges to change their votes. Find a vote that the Charter’s rule and a simple majority with the President’s tie-break decide differently.
slides.takeaway: At 2–2, with the President, the British judge, voting guilty, a simple majority would convict. But the Charter needed three votes, so there was no conviction.

slides.heading: Two voting rules in one court

left.label: Most decisions
left.text: A simple majority of the four judges. On a 2–2 tie, the President of the tribunal, Britain’s Geoffrey Lawrence, decided.

right.label: Convictions
right.text: At least three of the four judges had to vote guilty. A 2–2 split meant no conviction.

slides.question: At Nuremberg, the four judges split two against two on whether a defendant was guilty. What happened?
slides.explanation: The charter needed three votes to convict. Historians say all three acquittals at Nuremberg came from splits among the judges.
